summary: This is an April Fools' Day RFC. It humorously proposes that routing area documents include a morality section, claiming that neglecting morality has led to a decline in moral values on the Internet. It is a joke and not a serious requirement.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a joke document. It pretends that computer rules should include a section about being good, as if routers needed manners.

questions: what is the april fools joke in rfc 4041
subtitle: A joke proposal to require morality sections in routing drafts

tldr.problem: This is an April Fools' Day joke claiming that routing protocols lack moral consideration and have contributed to declining internet morality.
tldr.mechanism: It proposes that all routing area internet-drafts include a mandatory 'Morality Considerations' section with specific subsections addressing misuse and oversight.
tldr.outcome: This is humor and not a serious requirement. No real morality sections were added to routing protocols.

today: This is an April Fools' joke document from 2005. It remains on record as an Informational RFC, but no actual morality sections were ever required in routing protocols.

sections.title: The Joke Setup
sections.content:
This April Fools' Day RFC presents itself as a serious requirements document, but the entire point is humor. It claims that Internet protocols designed in the routing area have failed to consider morality, leading to declining moral values on the Internet itself. The RFC proposes that all future routing area internet-drafts must include a 'Morality Considerations' section to address this supposed crisis.

The document uses deadpan language and absurd logic throughout. For example, it suggests that the mere existence of routing protocols encourages immoral behavior, and that adding a morality section would somehow prevent this.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine if every science project needed to explain why it was a good idea. That's what this joke document proposes for computer networking rules.

sections.title: The Mandatory Subsections
sections.content:
The RFC lays out six mandatory subsections that must appear in any routing draft's morality section. These include considerations for misuse by 'depraved or sick individuals' and 'misguided individuals', while exempting certain high-status people from needing to write one at all. The RFC satirizes different groups: it mocks those with suspicious morals, implies that encryption should be banned for oversight, and even includes a humorous subsection on the care of avian carriers (referencing RFC 1149, which describes transmitting IP over carrier pigeons).

The requirement for these subsections is presented with false gravity, even stating that papers that consider some subsections irrelevant must still include them with a 'full rebuttal' of that deviant thought.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC lists silly things that every document supposedly must explain, like making sure your protocol won't be used for bad stuff—but in an over-the-top way.

sections.title: The Applicability Scenarios
sections.content:
The RFC then presents increasingly absurd 'applicability scenarios' where these morality requirements supposedly matter. It discusses Quality of Service in terms of 'sermons that contain strong moral messages'. Under the heading of Political Correctness, it makes jokes about terminology ('capacitorially challenged' instead of 'jumbo packets', 'packets of color' instead of segregating packets by color). It satirizes the internet's tendency toward euphemism and political correctness.

The section on 'Protection or Abstinence' uses crude double entendre about networking concepts like 1:1 and 1:n protection schemes. A final section on 'Promiscuity' dismisses promiscuous mode operation as immoral, ending with 'exceeded only by multicast'—treating networking concepts as if they had moral dimensions.
sections.plainLanguage: The document describes silly scenarios where networking concepts are treated as if they have morality, using jokes about not being 'promiscuous' with data and bad puns about network terms.

references.text: Bradner, S., "Key words for use in RFCs to Indicate Requirement Levels", BCP 14, RFC 2119, March 1997.
